utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, do you have something to contribute to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. With respect to the request of the Trial Chamber of yesterday regarding the constitution and the status of the death penalty in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I can report to you that, in fact, copies should be delivered soon of the current penal code of The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well as the constitution which was annexed to the Dayton agreement, which is the current constitution for the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I can report that the death penalty still is listed as a penalty in the Penal Code of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and in particular with respect to Articles 141 and 142, Articles dealing with genocide and war crimes committed against civilian populations. The constitution does not address the issue directly, but I will tell you that based on our research and some discussions it appears that it will be a question for the constitutional court in The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina whether the death penalty will still be applicable in the future, much as in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, because of the terms of the new constitution, but as of this date the penalty is still listed on the books, and, in fact, has been awarded in or adjudicated in cases involving war crimes after the adoption of the code in 1992. For example, one case in particular, the case of Borislov Herak, which was adjudicated on 3rd March 1993, in which he received the death penalty, along with Sretko Dajanovic, for war crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Will you provide us with a copy of that document as well? I don't know what you have, a verdict or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: We don't have a copy of the verdict, your Honour. That wasn't available to us. I can attempt to obtain a copy and provide that to the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Keegan. Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I listened carefully to the statement of Mr. Keegan and I wish to note that Bosnia-Herzegovina does not have a new Penal Code. It took over the old Penal Code of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and it is evident that the death penalty is listed there, but with the coming into force of the new constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the intention is that the death penalty can no longer exist as a criminal sanction, and that is why that Penal Code is in contradiction with the constitution and as such, according to constitutional law which is still in force in The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that law cannot be implemented, so that the Defence is of the opinion that it is quite evident that even the adjudicated sentences will not be implemented and will have to be corrected eventually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. To clarify the issue addressed, it stems from the provision in the constitution promulgated with the Dayton accords that says that the European Convention on Human Rights along with its two Optional Protocols will be enforced, the principles therein. I believe it is Optional Protocol 1 calls for the abolition of the death penalty. It allows states, however, to file reservations following certain procedural steps. The issue is The Republic of the Bosnia-Herzegovina has not stated it has accepted that European Convention and two Optional Protocols and consequently has not taken the step to file the reservation or not. The state could still file the reservation that makes the death penalty applicable for certain crimes. That step has not been taken which is why it is a question at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: With respect to the Penal Code. It may have been a matter of semantics. Mr. Vujin says The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina took over the old Penal Code.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: He is, in fact, correct. What the document you see shows on 11th April 1992 The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina adopted the Penal Code of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as its Penal Code.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay, and it provides for the death penalty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Exactly, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, do you have anything else on this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: No, your Honour, at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, you have provided the Defence with a copy of what you provided to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Copies were being made as I came down. They will be brought into the court and will be provided as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, yesterday we heard from the Prosecution. We received its submission regarding the appropriate sentence from its point of view and we are now to hear from the Defence. Are you ready to proceed? Are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, the Defence is ready, but if we can beg your indulgence, Mr. Livingston will start. After that, Mr. Kostic and I will come last. So we have shared amongst us certain segments of the statement so that we promise not to be repetitious, but we would all of us like to contribute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That is acceptable. How long do you anticipate you will require jointly?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Altogether perhaps two hours on the outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed. Mr. Livingston?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: May it please your Honours, I want to try and be realistic about this case. Let me say at the outset that I fully accept that this Defendant has been convicted of very serious offences, and I also accept that because of that this Trial Chamber has no option but to impose a substantial period of imprisonment. Let me also say right at the outset in respect of the comments made by Mr. Niemann yesterday concerning the Erdemovic case, that I fully accept that this is not a case where I can ask the Trial Chamber to give credit for a guilty plea; it's not a case where I can ask the Trial Chamber to give credit for remorse; and it's not a case, I think, where I can ask the Trial Chamber to give any great credit for co-operation with the authorities, though I was reminded yesterday afternoon that, in fact, Mr. Tadic did give some assistance by way of providing evidence. While he was in Germany, he made some statements relating to a case tried while he was there concerning a man called Gegic. It may be that others know more about that matter than I do, but. But in substance the matters that were in Mr. Erdemovic's favour in his circumstances were not available to this Defendant and I accept that. I said a substantial period of imprisonment must follow. The burning question, of course, is: how long? The emotional reaction to that question is liable to be something along the lines of: "The man's a monster. He must be locked up for life", but, of course, this Trial Chamber, consisting of professional Judges, must resist the emotional response and simply concern itself with matters of reason. As far as the guidance that the Trial Chamber is given by the statute and rules, of course that is well-known to you and it is limited. It is common ground that the starting point is Article 24, which, of course, entitles the Trial Chamber to send this Defendant to prison for life. In sub-Article 2 it emphasises that the Trial Chamber should take into account such factors as the gravity of the offence and the individual circumstances of the convicted person. I don't think, unless there's any serious argument to the contrary, I don't think sub-Article 3 about the return of property and proceeds is relevant to this particular case. The matter is elaborated on a little bit further, of course, in the rules. Rule 101 asks you to look at aggravating circumstances, mitigating circumstances, the general practice regarding prison sentences in the former Yugoslavia and also any penalty imposed by any other court. Again, that last matter is not, I think, of any relevance to this case. The only matter that is perhaps of some relevance is that this appellant has so far served some 3 years and 4 months in prison, if my arithmetic is correct. You are specifically, of course, asked to have regard, and I do stress the words "have regard", because I don't think it is in any way binding upon you, to have regard to the practice involving prison sentences in the former Yugoslavia and I think one ought to say straightaway that the Trial Chamber in Erdemovic did not find they had a lot of guidance about the actual practice as opposed to what the laws dictate as far as the former Yugoslavia is concerned, but it would nonetheless appear that similar factors must be borne in mind, such as the nature and circumstances of the offences, injury to victims, deterrents, personal circumstances of the Defendant and matters of that ilk. I'm not going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I just ask you a question? What in your submission is the relevant date at which one, as it were, freezes the law in the former Yugoslavia and looks at it? Is it the current law? Is it the law at the time of the offences?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Well, what I would suggest is -- let me say straightaway it may be my own obtuseness, but I found myself somewhat confused at the end of Professor Aleksic's evidence yesterday. I thought I knew a little bit about the law of Yugoslavia from the materials kindly supplied by Mr. Niemann, but what I would venture to suggest is that one should be looking at the law as it was, I think, in about 1992, because I think it's only sensible to face up to the fact that this Tribunal has the power to impose life imprisonment. If one does not face up to that, the Yugoslav law at present is not going to be of very much assistance. It seems the Yugoslav law at present is in a state of flux. If one accepts what Professor Aleksic says, the maximum at present is arguably 15 years. What I would submit is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: May I ask you a question just regarding that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I gather at the time, 1992, there was no provision for life imprisonment. The maximum was the death penalty and, of course, if the death penalty was not imposed, and if I'm intruding into an argument that is going to be presented by other counsel, tell me --

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: My question is -- even if someone else is going to respond to it, they can think about an answer in advance -- would there be a nullem crimen sine lege problem if the Tribunal imposes a life sentence, if the life sentence was not provided for in any of the republics of former Yugoslavia? In May 1992 there was not a provision. It was either death or a maximum of 15 years or 20 years, if I understood the Professor. Professors are wonderful, but sometimes it is a little difficult. Under certain circumstances the 20 year imprisonment could be imposed instead of a death penalty but no provision for life. Is there a nullem crimen problem, since the statute requires we have recourse to the sentencing practices in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Let me say straightaway Mr. Vujin is far better qualified to talk about Yugoslav law than I am. All I was going to say about Yugoslav law were two points. Without wishing to side step your Honour's question, perhaps I can make those points. The first one is that the 20 years seems to have been in some way regarded as an alternative in some cases to the death penalty. I think the Prosecutor's brief in Annex B, which you may well have to hand, points out, I think, quite usefully the way that the Yugoslav authorities looked at that 20 year term. I am looking particularly at page 3 of Annex B, which deals with the Penal Code in the former Yugoslavia, if you have it. It is paragraph 9, towards the bottom of the page. In fact, it's the last few lines, where it is observed that: "Further, 20 years' imprisonment was the limit of the alternative sanction, since in the SFRY it was assumed that a sentence longer than 20 years in jail, particularly a life sentence, was far more cruel than death". That's the first point I was going to make. The second point is I think that one thing I did pick up quite clearly from Professor Aleksic's evidence was that both the death penalty and the 20 year alternative would only be imposed in what were regarded as exceptional cases, and there are two points I would make about the word "exceptional". The first one is this, that in its definition, in my submission, it contains the idea of rarity, because if there were a lot of offences of that particular type, then, in my submission, it would not be exceptional. I think that's important in the context of a case like this, because sadly because of the war and the circumstances -- the breakdown of law and order in Bosnia there were a lot of cases like this, and indeed there are a lot of cases which are frankly, and I don't think Mr. Niemann would argue with this, which are considerably worse than this. One only has to look at the other outstanding indictments to see that. The circumstances had to be exceptional, and can I deal with that in two ways? One, the exceptionality of the offence itself, and, secondly, the exceptionality of the offender. I have already made the point that this is not, even on the Prosecution submission to you, this is not the worst example to you of either a crime against humanity or war crimes, which this Tribunal will see. The second point is this, that there is nothing, in my submission, intrinsic to the term "crime against humanity" and I am concentrating primarily on count 1, because I think that is frankly the most serious offence by far which you have to deal with, and that's not to minimise the other matters, there is nothing intrinsic in a crime against humanity which demands that you impose a sentence of life imprisonment. That might seem a trite point. I make it because, as the Trial Chamber may be aware, in the country where I practice if somebody is convicted of murder, the life sentence is mandatory. There are no other option available to the court at all unless there are other factors such as mental illness. The life sentence is mandatory and then it is for the Trial Judge these days to recommend what he thinks would be an appropriate minimum term which the Defendant should serve before he is eligible to apply for parole. That's the way it works, but with a crime against humanity it doesn't seem as though that's the position, and there's ample authority for that which your colleagues in the Erdemovic case amply set out. Of the 22 Defendants who were tried in Nuremberg, 12 of them got the ultimate penalty of the death penalty; the others didn't, with varying other sentences being imposed. Equally, of course, in the Erdemovic case again, where there was one count of a crime against humanity, again no life imprisonment sentence was imposed; indeed none was asked for by the Prosecution. So there's nothing intrinsic in Count 1 which obliges you, in my submission, to say that it's so exceptional that life imprisonment should follow. One has to look then at the nature of the offences, the circumstances of the offences. I am not going to say anything about the facts of this case. That wouldn't be appropriate. You have already expressed your findings on those in considerable depth, and are far more familiar with them, frankly, than I am. What I will say is this, that I think one has to consider those acts in their context and there are two aspects to that, I suggest. Firstly, that this is an internationally condemned conflict in Bosnia, condemned both by the UN and European Parliament and other bodies. Secondly, it's a conflict which even in the view of many hardened war correspondents was particularly brutal and nasty. Unfortunately it wasn't that short, but it was particularly brutal and nasty. The second point about it is the matter or the matters which you yourselves found in your judgement, and I particularly have in mind the passages which start at paragraph 87 of the judgement. It is there that you set out your findings about how nationalism built up in Serbia, then in Bosnia, and at paragraph 89 you mention a man called Radoslav Brdanin, who was at that time President of the crisis staff in Banja Luka, setting out what he advocated about ethnic cleansing and creating impossible conditions that would have the effect of encouraging non-Serbs to leave, deportation and banishment, liquidating those remaining. Then there is a statement in the next paragraph 90 relating to Colonel Vukalic, where you record that he characterised Croats and Muslims as the enemies of Serbs and proclaimed that Serbs in Bosnia were in danger and needed to be protected. Then you point out in paragraph 91 about the propaganda escalating in intensity, and so it goes on. Perhaps the way you sum up that evidence which you accepted is recorded in paragraph 69 in the quotation from Edward Vulliamy, the British journalist. You record there that the message from the government in Belgrade was relentless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Did you say 69?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: 96. I beg your pardon. I think I maybe did say 69. 96. You record there that you accept what he said: "The message from the government in Belgrade was relentless, cogent and potent, a message of urgency, a threat to your people, to your nation, a call to arms, and yes, a sort of instruction to go to war for your people. It pushed and pushed." One of the points that was made in the Erdemovic case, and I'm thinking particularly of paragraph 60, and at paragraph 60 in the Erdemovic decision the Trial Chamber there were analysing the purposes and functions of national criminal systems in their sentencing process and they record similar factors as one finds evidently in Yugoslav law, the prevention of recidivism, deterrents and retribution, the three elements, which they say are attenuated in the contemporary version by the principle that punishment shall be appropriate to the crime's gravity and the moral guilt of the perpetrator. It's that phrase, moral guilt, which I think one must not lose sight of in this case, because when you assess the seriousness of these crimes, in my submission those who bear the greater responsibility for creating the wave of nationalism which you found is the background to these offences, those who bear the greater responsibility for creating that wave, and those who give orders for the commission of these offences must bear the greater responsibility for them and should be punished more severely. In moral terms, in my submission, that must be the case. In terms of the hierarchy in Republika Srpska, let alone, of course, Serbia, Mr. Tadic, in my submission, comes very much at the bottom of the pile. I'll leave Serbia on one side, but, of course, there are the national leaders in Bosnia. There are people like Mr. Brdanin. There's the other gentleman who is referred to in the Prosecutor's brief, Radoslav Vukic, described as being the President of the SDS committee in Banja Luka. There are also all the journalists. There is Simo Miskovic, a name with which you will be familiar, the President of the SDS in the Prijedor area; Milomir Stakic, who was, I , think rather more local but equally had Presidential status, and even in the Kozarac area at the time these offences were committed, the President of the Serbian Assembly was a man called Dragicevic. So at every level this appellant comes at the bottom of the pile. I accept, of course, your findings that he was to some extent an SDS activist, and you have recorded that you found that he helped organise the plebiscite, the Serbian plebiscite in Kozarac area. I accept that, but one shouldn't overestimate the part that he played in the nationalistic movement which had built up. It was others who were primarily responsible for stirring up those background circumstances. You have recorded that the media bear a substantial responsibility for fermenting that nationalism, and at the end of the day Mr. Tadic comparatively, and I say carefully, again to use prosecution terminology, in my submission can be seen as a relatively little fish. Again I don't want to belittle the acts which you have found him to have played in that movement, but relatively speaking he is not, in my submission, to any substantial degree responsible for the whipping up of that atmosphere which you found existed at the time. What I suggest realistically happened here, and I make this point, because a lot of people might say: how do you reconcile the evidence of Ms. Metselaar and the Tadic family with the findings that you have made that Mr. Tadic committed such grave offences, and in my submission the only way that one can reconcile those findings with the other evidence which you have heard, which I submit is credible evidence, is that this was a man who, like watching, as I did the other night, the waves rolling in over the beach in Scheveningen, he was swept along by that wave of nationalism. I am not trying in any way to say that he was compelled to do what you found, but he was swept along in that wave of nationalism, the sort of speeches which I have reminded you of and which are recorded in the Prosecutor's brief. It's in that light that one can fairly conclude, in my submission, that it is wholly wrong to characterise this man as a monster, as some do. He's a man who is plainly a beloved husband, a beloved father, inspiring great loyalty not only in his family but in a number of friends in Republika Srpska, but perhaps Ms. Metselaar's evidence is really terribly significant, because she is an independent person. You would expect, perhaps, that the family might be somewhat biased in his favour. Ms. Metselaar is not. She is a fellow Serb, but otherwise she came with an open mind. You will recall the way she summed him up as in her judgement, and she has been in regular contact with him for two years, as a caring and sensitive man. It may be that the paintings which you have seen put before you perhaps bear out that he is a caring and sensitive man. He's not a man who takes lightly the kindness which he has received from the diaspora Serb community, but again you heard from Ms. Metselaar in her particular case he sends her Christmas cards, birthday cards, New Year's cards, the little things he can do in his position. He can't do much to respond. In respect of every person who sent him money or clothes, she told you he sends them letters to thank them. This is not a man who is a monster. This is a man who is capable of great good and who has done good in his life. One must not ignore the fact -- I know Mr. Niemann says he is two-faced -- one must not ignore the fact that he was also involved in Republika Srpska in distributing humanitarian aid for the Red Cross, again something to his credit. He taught karate at a local club to young students, young people in his area. These are not the marks of a man who is the sort of monster, whom some people would say is the picture presented by your findings in this case. What I submit is that one must look at his acts in the context of this background material, what I have described as the wave of nationalism, the whipping up of anti-Croat and Muslim feeling, which you have found existed as a background to these events and indeed to the war in Bosnia as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Livingston, before you move on to another point, perhaps, I would like to ask you a question about, I guess, the big fish and the little fish. I don't know how to put it any better. The reason I'm asking you this question is I know this is a question that goes in my mind and so I want to share it with you so perhaps you can respond and help me, because you will not be with me when I'm thinking about it. You are correct about the findings in the Opinion and Judgement recognising that there were competing claims for nationalism from both sides, Croatia and Serbia, and I hope that point has been made clear in the judgement. Those persons who are mentioned by name have not been indicted even. Some of the people who you mention as playing a larger role and perhaps bearing more responsibility for stirring up these nationalistic feelings, which go beyond nationalism it would seem to me, but in any case some of those people have been indicted, but those people have not been tried yet, and so they are presumed innocent until such time as they are found guilty beyond reasonable doubt. Sometimes we hear, you know, people say: "What about the big fish? You are not doing anything. Go get the big fish". The implication is the big fish, whoever they may be, by whose standards -- perhaps victims look at it differently -- assuming they are, that's not the role of a Judge. Personally I do not get involved in that dialogue and suggest that somehow we are responsible for getting the big fish. My job is to, as I view it, try individuals who appear before me and make a determination, based on the evidence, as to whether the Prosecution has proved beyond reasonable doubt that they are guilty and leave everything else to the extent that I can as a human being who reads and watches TV, leave those things out of my mind. So now how can I plug that in and say: "Well, you know, there are people out there, some of whom have been indicted, some of whom have not been indicted, but whom I believe, notwithstanding the fact that they have not been tried, I believe that they are more guilty, so I want to save this most extreme penalty for them". How do I handle that when I am thinking about these subjects?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: This Tribunal, this Trial Chamber, has -- let me say straightaway I am not being, I hope, patronising to any -- it is a very difficult task in deciding how to sentence a case like this. You have very little guidance to go on because this is only the second case where a Defendant has fallen to be sentenced, but the reason I touched on that point was because the Prosecution themselves in their brief -- it's on the second page. They start off one of their main paragraphs by saying: "Tadic was not a little fish". It is for that reason that I broached the subject at all. It does appear to me that the only way one can deal with that sort of allegation is to point out that there are a lot of other people, whoever they may be, and maybe it is not fair to mention names, because those people might say: "I didn't do that. I'm not guilty". I understand your point. The reality is there are national leaders and there are minor party activists at the other end and there are people in between, whoever they are. They exist. The media do exist. Public pronouncements have been made. I think whatever one says about the people I named, as I understand the Prosecution case, they are simply quoting from what is in the public forum, and what I do say to you is you cannot ignore words that are spoken by whoever in the public forum, forum, in the media, on major public platforms, and one cannot ignore the effect that those statements and what is coming through on the television creates. There is another passage in your judgement which I cannot immediately identify, where you indicate there came a time when in the Republika Srpska they could only receive television from Serbia. You have made findings about the role played by Serbia in this atmosphere. One cannot ignore the effect on public opinion, the way people think, which the power of the media helps to create. All I am trying to say is Mr. Tadic did very little to create that atmosphere. He lived in a small town in Bosnia and he was not a person who was making major public speeches on the radio or the television. He was not primarily somebody who was responsible for creating this background, and that is the reason why I would invite you to the conclusion that it is fair to regard him as a little fish, even though, of course, other bigger fishes may or may not have been indicted and certainly have not been tried. You are in a situation where you have to sentence this man now, but one must, in my submission, look at his moral guilt, and that means looking at his place in the hierarchy, where his level truly is. I don't think you can simply ignore the fact that there are many other people in the background who bear in my submission a bigger responsibility than he does for creating the atmosphere in Bosnia in which the war was fought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I was thinking in my system it might fit something like an unindicted co-conspirator, something like that. The person out there pulling the strings, not indicted doing some very evil things. You left out the quote when reference was made to the second gentleman that he said that the children of mixed marriages were only good for making soap. So there is some pretty dastardly remarks there in that section.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: They are dastardly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Made by leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Precisely. Your Honour and your colleagues have made those findings, but one must consider the impact of those sort of statements on what I suggest is the ordinary man in Bosnia, such as Mr. Tadic, and one cannot, I would submit, just ignore the power of the media in that context, and I would invite you to look very carefully in the way I have suggested at his true moral guilt, and the true responsibility which it is right to let him bear for what he did in the light of the atmosphere that had been found created. Perhaps I can just move on to finish what I was saying, if I may, about Mr. Tadic being a man who has good in him. You are going to hear, of course, tomorrow from Dr Nedopil, but I think perhaps I can sum up his report, I hope not unfairly, in about one sentence, which is that he saw nothing in Mr. Tadic's character, as he saw it, which would indicate that he was a man who was inclined by nature to commit the sort of acts which have been found proved in this case. So in so far as the relevance of my being able to say that they are out of character is concerned and the likelihood of anything like this ever happening again, then his report is in line with Ms. Metselaar that these offences do not square with his character and his nature as the psychiatrist observed it to be. Your Honour, I have dealt, I hope, with the issue about a crime of humanity not being intrinsically one where one has to impose life imprisonment. I have dealt, I hope, with the circumstances in which the offences were committed. I have started on this question of Mr. Tadic's own character, and I would ask you to bear that in mind. I would also ask you to bear in mind the effect on his family, and I think particularly on the young girl Valentina. It doesn't need much imagination, I would have thought, to reach the conclusion that what has happened to her father must be like dropping an atom bomb in her life, and whatever courage, whatever courageous appearance she can put on that, it must be devastating. I think to any parent being able to observe, as Mr. Tadic does, that devastation in a child, and also, of course, in his wife and his nearest and dearest is very painful, and I think it's only right that you should take that into account as well. Can I also deal with another aspect of this case, and this primarily goes to the documents which I'm afraid I was responsible for being handed in yesterday. I think it's known as Exhibit 120. They are documents which look like this. What I would ask you to bear in mind, because I do think it's important, is that whatever sentence you impose on Mr. Tadic, that's not going to be the end of the punishment which he faces, because my submission to you is that his life is ruined for the rest of his days, and I say that for this reason, that you have had evidence put before you -- Mr. Vujin put it in the other day -- that he has been summonsed or there is an indictment or a charge, whatever the proper term is in the Republika Srpska, for him for avoidance of military service. It is to that point that these documents I would now ask you to look at go. I know it is perhaps a little bit illogical to ask you to take the documents out of order, but the second document in that bundle is a report dated December 1996 by UNHCR. I have extracted merely one page from it. I don't think for these purposes I have taken it out of context. The passages, I think, you have to pay attention to are those I have marked in the margin. I hope you can see the markings. It refers to the fact that there is -- well, I think it's well-known that the Dayton Agreement actually obliged all the participants in the conflicts in Yugoslavia to pass amnesties in respect of people who avoided military service. They have all done so except Republika Srpska. That page from the UNHCR report bears that out. The first passage I have marked said: "It is widely agreed that the national amnesty law for the whole of Bosnia does not and will not apply in Republika Srpska". Then the second passage: "The Republika Srpska amnesty law does not mention the criminal offence of calling for resistance and specifically excludes from the amnesty those who have committed the criminal acts of not responding to the call-up or avoiding military service and wilful escape or desertion from the army". The following document, Article 2 is the article which sets that out specifically. The translation comes first and the original for anybody who can read the language follows. The document at the back again is another document which emanates from UNHCR, dated 31st August 1994. You can see what the punishments are for draft evasion on -- it's the second page of the document, of that particular letter, under the heading "What is the Punishment the Bosnia Government can Impose on Draft Evaders/Deserters?" The answer is: "In time of war persons convicted of refusing/avoiding military obligation are liable to imprisonment for one to ten years if they are still in Bosnia, or imprisonment for five to fifteen years or death if they have left the country". Then on the final page the passage again I have marked says this: "They also advise", that is UNHCR's office in Sarajevo, "that many of the human rights issues in Bosnia resolve around mobilisation, and there is no doubt that persons who try to avoid military service are seen as traitors and face problems ranging from harassment to persecution to possible attempts on their life". I read that last passage because even if an amnesty law is passed, there remains a significant remaining problem, which is again dealt with perhaps best in the first letter in that bundle, that by Florin Gomel from the European Bureau for Conscientious Objection. I pause, because I don't know whether His Honour Judge Stephen wished to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I will in a moment, but you carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Again I have marked for you, I hope, the relevant passages in that letter. What it's saying is -- although I, of course, accept that it places particular emphasis on the difficulties which those from mixed families, mixed ethnic origins come, it says: "Despite the apparent removal of the risk of prosecution", that's particularly in Serbia and in the federation part of Bosnia, "I would agree with the comment made by the European Civic Forum in the article which you kindly sent me that such people, especially those from mixed families, are likely to be the victims of extra-legal treatment, which would amount to persecution within the 1951 Geneva Convention on Refugees. This persecution would be likely to take the form of social discrimination, i.e. denial of access to available housing, employment opportunities, administrative harassment and rejection by their communities". It also points out that paramilitary influence is still a powerful influence particularly in Bosnia, and physical attacks by ultra-nationalistic groups are sadly still a possibility. That was in September of last year. So the point I am making is, however long this man has to serve in prison he is going to come out at some stage. He's going to have difficulties, in my submission, in his homeland of Republika Srpska. That's what those documents, in my submission, would indicate. In my submission, he's going to have very great difficulty if he attempts to go elsewhere. Imagine, and this is not intended as a frivolous comment, imagine him going to a foreign country and trying to get work, even assuming he can speak their language. What does he put on his curriculum vitae? Because of his position as the first person who has been tried before this Tribunal, he is going to find it quite impossible to build a life anywhere else outside Bosnia. His position, in a nutshell, in my submission is almost an impossible one outside Republika Srpska or inside Republika Srpska. That is why I say that you shouldn't assume that his punishment is going to end with whatever this court imposes. It is something which will continue for the rest of his days. I know that it could be said that he has brought it on himself, granted the findings of facts that you have made, but the reality is that he is going to pay the penalty for it not just in a prison cell, but thereafter. Even while he is in prison, of course, his circumstances are likely to be more difficult than perhaps the average prisoner's. You will recall, I'm sure, what was said in the Erdemovic case. It's at page 36. It's paragraph 75 where the Trial Chamber made this observation: "In addition, because persons found guilty will be obliged to serve their sentences in institutions which are often far from their places of origin, the Trial Chamber takes note of the inevitable isolation into which they will have been placed. Moreover, cultural and linguistic differences will distinguish them from the other detainees". So wherever he goes, and I take note of what was said yesterday about Italy and Finland being currently the only two countries which have made the appropriate agreements in this regard, wherever he goes, he is going to suffer any term of imprisonment in a state of some isolation. It may be worse, and you may say this is fanciful, but I think it isn't, because I think it's known that Mr. Tadic has already been the subject of one assault while he has been in custody, it may be in a foreign jail that he will find it very difficult in prison. One has seen the attitude on one occasion, when he has been in custody here and, of course, if that happens, it may be that he will have to serve his sentence in solitary confinement. That is to some extent speculation, but I do ask you to bear in mind that there has already been one incident, and that it may be an indication sadly of things to come. My main point is the point made in the Erdemovic case that inevitably, because he serves a sentence abroad, in a country where he won't speak the language, inevitably isolation is an important factor, and it's also a factor that his family will find it difficult to visit him if he's in prison in a foreign country. Can I deal briefly with the subject of concurrent and consecutive sentences? I rather suspect, although it's a very difficult problem in many cases, I rather suspect that it may not be a problem that troubles this court greatly, but the system in English law is one which I hope may commend itself to this Trial Chamber. It is very simply this. I will just find the appropriate passage. I beg your pardon. The system basically is this, that one should look first of all and primarily at the totality of the sentences which one is imposing; in other words, to see whether the aggregate sentence is just and appropriate, taking the offences as a whole, the totality principle, but one of the circumstances which is specified and I am reading from the leading practitioner's textbook on English criminal law, Archbold’s Criminal Pleading Evidence and Practice. It is the 1997 edition. This is at paragraph 5-150. One of the circumstances which is set out there for imposing a concurrent sentence is where an offender who is sentenced to a long-term of imprisonment for a grave crime is also liable to be sentenced to shorter terms for some other matter or matters. Without wishing in any way to belittle the other offences other than Count 1, in my submission it may well be that the court would have in mind that the principal sentence in this case would be for Count 1 in which case I would invite you to follow that principle, that the appropriate course is then to make the other sentences run concurrently. I would also say -- I think Mr. Kostic will also say something more about this -- I would also say that you should have regard to the fact that these offences, while not obviously all committed on one occasion or on one day, do in a sense form a course of conduct over a period of time, and they are all committed in one comparatively small area. It's not as though, for example, Mr. Tadic went off to Belgrade and committed some offences there. These are offences which are all confined to Opstina Prijedor and are all within a few months. If you take the view that they are properly to be regarded as a course of conduct, then that is something which would go in favour of imposing concurrent sentences for the other offences apart from that in Count 1. Your Honour, finally, can I deal with the moral message? I don't want to sound pompous when I say this -- the moral message which I think this Tribunal has, certainly something which was dealt with in Erdemovic. I would accept that the message which has to go out to Yugoslavia and the world is that those who commit crimes against humanity and war crimes have to expect to be dealt with severely. That's the first important message. The second message is a different one, and perhaps I can be excused, and I hope again I am not going to cause problems for the interpreters, but I think it's a message which is expressed by Shakespeare more eloquently than I can ever express it. I hope the Tribunal will bear with me if I simply quote two or three lines from the famous speech of Portia's in the Merchant of Venice towards the end of Act IV. You may recall at that point that Portia has said to Shylock that: "The Jew must be merciful". His answer is: "Upon what compulsion must I be merciful?" The answer which she gives towards the end of the famous speech is this: "Therefore, Jew," she says, "though justice be thy plea, consider this: that in the course of justice none of us should see salvation. We do pray for mercy and that same prayer doth teach us all to render the deeds of mercy". I do submit to you that that's a message which it is equally important that this Tribunal sends out to Yugoslavia and to the world. Justice is a severe concept which catches up with all of us, again to quote Portia's speech: "... unless it is seasoned with mercy". I particularly make this point, because there are some, and I'm sure you are well aware of this, who see this Tribunal's function as an avenging angel for whichever ethnic group is the victim in any particular case. That, of course, as you readily accept, is not the function of this Tribunal, to be seen as an avenging angel. It wasn't just Portia or Shakespeare through her who expressed this point. It was also a matter which the Tribunal in Erdemovic -- the Trial Chamber in Erdemovic dealt with at page 21 of the judgement, paragraph 46. They quoted there from the decision of the United States Military Tribunal when it delivered its sentence in the famous hostage case. It's the top of page 21. The relevant part of the quotation is this: "The degree of mitigation depends upon many factors, including the nature of the crime, the age and experience of the person to whom it applies, the motives for the criminal act, the circumstances under which the crime was committed, and the provocation, if any, that contributed to its commission". Then they put in italics these words: "It must be observed, however, that mitigation of punishment does not in any sense of the word reduce the degree of the crime. It is more a matter of grace than of defence". In my submission again that is harking back to what Shakespeare wrote so many centuries ago: justice is not justice unless there is an element of grace and of mercy which is shown. I invite you in closing my submissions to you to send that message out not to encourage the avenging angel concept, that the message that justice involves and should be tempered by mercy and grace is an important one, and is something that should be regarded widely as a principle for those who commit crimes such as Mr. Tadic has been convicted of and others who may be in the future. I invite you to show him mercy for the reasons which I have given, to bear in mind his personal circumstances, to bear in mind that this is not the worst offence of its kind, and I would invite you not to go down the route of imposing life imprisonment. I would invite you to pose a determinate sentence on this still relatively young man -- I think he's one year older than me. Of course, as I said at the outset, it must be a substantial one, but it should be one in accordance with the principles of United States law, which are set out in the Prosecutor's brief: sufficient but not greater than necessary. I would ask you to remember the way the Yugoslavs themselves regard that 20 year term, only to be imposed in exceptional cases, exceptional cases, because they regard more than 20 years as being worse than the death penalty. I would invite you to take all the mitigating factors into account that I've mentioned to reduce that sentence as much as you feel able to do. Your Honour, unless I can assist you further, those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Livingston. Mr. Vujin, will you proceed next?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Mr. Kostic will proceed next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I am trying to get set up here. May it please your Honours, Mr. Niemann, Mr. Keegan, colleagues of the defence, it's been pretty rare in my career to come in and argue a case at the very tail end; in other words, the sentencing portion, when so much has occurred before I step up. I can make some comparisons, something to the effect of coming in and putting in one brick when a house is built and then stepping back and reviewing my work and reviewing the work of everybody else. You have built a house here. You have built a trial, you have built a procedure, you have built a process, a legal process. I say that because I want you to understand my comments and perhaps I'm also doing some preventative work, saying there may be some facts that the court knows much better than this attorney, which is true, in regard to this case, and of course my colleagues across the way on the Prosecution. But nevertheless Mr. Tadic, who is our client at the present time, was arrested on February 12th, 1994 in Munich, Germany. As you know, he had fled from his home town, from his area where he grew up and sought refuge. In the meanwhile unfortunately the war in Bosnia raged. The International Tribunal at some point was set up. May of 1993 is my recollection. He was arrested pursuant to some of the activities concerning investigations. It was the first time, to my knowledge, that Germany used a concept of universal jurisdiction for events that did not occur in Germany when he was arrested and when he was going to be tried in Germany. Then unfortunately for Mr. Tadic, he began recording firsts and has continued to record firsts in regard to his dealings with the legal system. He was the first person who was brought to The Hague in front of this Tribunal. He appeared here on April 26th, 1995 at an arraignment or initial hearing. He was the first person who became the guest at the UN detention centre. He was the first person who was litigating motions in front of your Tribunal and then even taking interlocutory appeals to the Appellate Chamber, the first person to be tried in a full trial and first person to be sentenced after a full trial. As you know, of course, a notice of appeal was filed in regard to the judgement of the court and, of course, that will be the first appeal. I don't think that Dusko Tadic would have ever wanted to record all of these firsts, but unfortunately he did. We have to deal with it. One of the things that I wanted to talk about just a little bit and, you know, when you go second, as I do, you have the benefit of Mr. Livingston breaking some of the ice hopefully, and also to hear what he has been asked and perhaps to even predict what some of the Judges may be thinking about. One of the thoughts that came across during his discourse was based on a question by Judge McDonald and talked about how Mr. Tadic fits into this system and then I think a greater part of the question, and that is this is the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia. What message do we send out? How do we judge each individual appearing in front of us? Do we only judge that individual? Is that individual judged in a vacuum, so to speak? By the way I don't think -- I am not paraphrasing the court correctly. That may not be the right terminology. Do we only look at his position in front of the court? Do we only look at the charge? Do we only look at the indictment? Do we only look at his role and function in what occurred in Bosnia in 1992 and 1993?, and so on. In the Erdemovic case some place in paragraph 58, and this comes from a report of the Tribunal itself, there is a discussion which essentially goes into the area and I cite here that: "The Tribunal is interested or concerned about the impunity of the guilt and whether that would only fuel the desire for vengeance in the former Yugoslavia, jeopardising the return to the rule of law, reconciliation and the restoration of true peace". So that seems to set some thoughts about the message that goes out from the Tribunal. I can tell you that I, like other people who have an interest in Yugoslavia, who are international lawyers, who are statesmen, who are Diplomats, have paid attention to how this Tribunal came into being. I believe that all of you in the Trial Chamber probably know that better than I do, but I have certain quotes in my mind as I recall the media, as I recall the jurists talking about this problem, the statesmen, politicians, who talked about whether or not there ought to be an international criminal tribunal for Yugoslavia, and once one was organised, what it would mean. I'm going to give you some random quotations. For example, one Professor thought that the Tribunal is a fig leaf for the international community's inaction during the war in Bosnia. Somebody said that the Tribunal is the single most important factor in whether the delicate truths in Bosnia hammered out in Dayton will hold. Other people thought the issue is whether or not people will be held to the standards of the 1949 Geneva Convention and the 1948 Genocide Convention. Somebody else talked about that the creation of the Tribunal is a dramatic development in the area of human rights because it called for the accountability of leaders of oppressive regimes. As a corollary to that quote: "You can't move forward and try to rebuild a society", talking about Bosnia and Herzegovina, "when you have the ringleaders of an oppressive regime in charge". Other quotes: the Tribunal being watched by proponents and opponents of the permanent court, in other words the thought that this Tribunal will be a model for a permanent court. I will not bore you with any more, because I suspect you have all a number of these types of quotations and citations that you have heard about. I just want to go -- I do want to give you one more quote and then see how Dusko Tadic fits into that. When the Tribunal was organised and Mr. Tadic, I think, had not been arrested at that point yet, and there were certain discussions about what the Tribunal would do and what it can do and what are the prospects for the Tribunal, one of the Judges was asked: "What happened when you came to the Tribunal?" That Judge said: "Initially there were 11 Judges, 3 secretaries and nothing. We had no jurisprudence we could rely upon": this citation is from Judge McDonald. I am not sure if I am quoting the Judge correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I don't read my own press.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Then you trust me that I am correct with that. One final quote in that regard. Now we are getting closer to the trial here of Mr. Tadic and somebody I think from the Prosecution staff said: "If the trial is conducted fairly and a decision is acceptable as a fair one, it will be a large boost for the formation of a permanent court". I don't think that person is interested in a permanent court. I trust that he was more interested in this trial being a fair one and being perceived as a fair one. So in a way Mr. Tadic, when he came along, this was the atmosphere. When I listened again, and I'm not sure if there was a colloquy between Judge Stephen and Mr. Livingston about this fish business, whether he was a little fish, big fish or whatever, I'm reminded of something. Again I am going to try to quote Judge Stephen at this time and then maybe I should quit quoting Judges. After the judgement in this case I watched an interview with Judge Stephen on one of the programmes and I think the Judge was asked that specific question: "Don't you think that Dusko Tadic is a little fish?" I think the Judge and for the fear of misquoting him I think this is what he said. He said: "I don't know about that, but he was the only fish", in other words, he was the only prisoner, he was the only one who was going to be tried. So in that regard Mr. Tadic has served a function here. It's my understanding from everything that I have read about the case and everything that I have seen on monitors and everything that I have watched myself -- as you know, this case received some publicity and some notice -- Mr. Tadic behaved well, courteously and assisted his defence. I'm not here at all to comment on how the trial was run. I'm not here to give an opinion whether it was a fair trial, whether he was dependent on the best acts of anybody, whether the government of the Republika Srpska co-operated or not. Those are things you know better than I do. I do think Mr. Tadic, the way he handled himself and the way he reacted to this court, did everything he could to be a gentleman and to handle himself properly. I also wanted to find a few things that the Prosecution and I could agree upon, because that's always very nice if we can agree on some things, because you then perhaps will take some of those agreements as a fact. I don't think that the Prosecution has any objection that under Rule 101E the credit for time that Mr. Tadic has been incarcerated be credited to him. I believe the actual figure at this point is 41 plus months. As far as Rule 101(C) --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Excuse me. Are you including time spent in Germany? I think in Mr. Livingston's calculation I guess he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was. From February 12th of 1994 until let's say today's date. That's as close as I can come. I'm sure that that will change depending on what happens from now on in terms of the 14th being the time for the actual pronouncement of the sentence and then if the appeal continues, of course, we don't know, but I don't think the Prosecution has any -- I have not heard any objection to that particular credit. Rule 101(C) talks about consecutive or concurrent sentences. I'm sure that Mr. Niemann will jump up if I misquote him or say something that he didn't mean yesterday. I understood him to say that this is an appropriate case for concurrent sentences. I heartily agree. Mr. Livingston had touched upon the fact that the concept is that Count 1 encompasses and subsumes all of the allegations -- initially all the allegations and, of course, now all of the counts that the court found Mr. Tadic to have committed, in other words found him guilty, that all of those events or incidents occurred between May 23rd, 1992 to December 31st, 1992, as is stated in Count 1 of the indictment. That is my understanding. In other words, that is the main count. I know that only Judge McDonald shares with me the American experience, although the other Judges may have read about it -- I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: My experience may be different than yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Let us see if that is true. It sounds to me, Judge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: You mean legally subsumes or factually subsumes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Factually, but I would compare it to a federal law in the United States which takes into consideration all of the planning, all of the scheme, all of the design, all of the facade of a common scope or a plan. Then you have additional counts which we call substantive counts, which are pieces or parcels of that scheme. That is the analogy that I would like to give to the court, because again I think it's the same course of conduct, and I think it's charged that way in the indictment. Now, not everything in Count 2 -- maybe overt acts -- were actually proved up and you have very nicely set out in your judgement which you thought was proved up and which was not. We know what it is. Then we have the remaining ten counts, which talk about activity and then, of course, convictions for specific acts which are mentioned generally under Count 1. That is the reason why I feel that a concurrent sentence is what ought to occur here. I think it looks like my colleague from England agrees at least in regard to English law with the Federal Law in the United States, and again I think Mr. Niemann agrees with that. He hasn't jumped up yet, so I'm feeling pretty good about it. So I think that's the situation on the concurrent and consecutive sentences. I would like to talk a little bit about the Erdemovic case and some of the language in there, because I have some thoughts and I have looked at the clock. What would you like, your Honour, in that regard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Perhaps we might take a recess now, but as you review your notes, recall what Mr. Livingston -- I apologise, Mr. Livingston -- what Mr. Livingston said about Erdemovic, so keep that in mind rather than repeating what he said. We expect that we will finish the submissions of the Defence today. We plan to proceed until 5.30. Perhaps, if necessary, if we will need to go a little bit later. In any case, we would like to finish the Defence submissions today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Judge, I have looked and listened and I will try very hard not to be redundant. I appreciate what you are telling me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I leave with this question for you; do I understand what you are saying on concurrent that the Count 1 sentence, because it subsumes all the incidents in the subsequent counts on which Mr. Tadic was found guilty, the rest should all be made concurrent with Count 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: If there are a number, one does not add them up and find they come to perhaps a longer term, a greater term than the term imposed under Count 1. One simply has them there on the record, but it would be the Count 1 sentence that's the effective one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would suggest, and I'm not suggesting this number, by the way, and please do not hold me to number -- I am doing this purely hypothetically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Let us make it X.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: If it is number X on Count 1 and Y and Z on the other counts, the sentences begin running at the same time, so the shorter sentences will expire and if sentence X on Count 1 is the longest, that will be the longest term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I don't want to go back to Professor Aleksic's business about "aspiration".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: No. You have the appropriate legislation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If your Honour, if you would like to take them with you on the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Why don't you pass it up? Prosecution Exhibit 374 will then be admitted. It is the criminal law of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. No objection, I gather, Mr. Vujin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. Very good. We will stand in recess for 20 minutes. Then when we return, we will continue with Mr. Kostic. (4.05 pm) (Short break) (4.25 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. Before I begin the argument, I wanted to inform you, because it was in the Erdemovic decision that I was looking at at the break, I think it is everybody's understanding that the countries of Finland and Italy have accepted agreements. I was also in paragraph 1 informed that a number of other countries apparently have applied -- I guess that would be the right word -- it is Denmark, Germany, Iran, Pakistan, the Netherlands, Sweden, Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. So that's a complete list. I'm sure we will be notified as to which of the applications are accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Some have agreed also to accept but with reservations that really affect the accomplishment of the incarceration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOSTIC
utterances.text: I only brought that up, your Honour, because there was some discussion about that by Mr. Livingston as to the situation concerning conditions, paroles, remissions and things of that nature, although it's my belief that Rule 104 seems to see that the Tribunal continues and shall have jurisdiction no matter what occurs in regard to any of the pardon, clemency or other issues. In listening to some of the comments of the Prosecutor in regard to Erdemovic I want to just bring a few facts out for your consideration. I want to be brief with that, because I think in some ways there is an invitation for you to draw some comparisons. To be very, very candid with the court, I'm struggling myself, as I read that decision and am involved in this case, to reconcile these decisions, to look at the legal theories behind the sentencing of the other gentleman by the other Trial Chamber. The concepts that Mr. Niemann talks about, the remorse concept, the mitigation factors, co-operation with the Prosecution, are not concepts that are -- I mean, they are common to all legal systems, and I'm having a difficult time reconciling, because I read the judgement in this case and other things, and then I have read, for example, in the Erdemovic case, that what we are dealing with pursuant to paragraph 78 and in that area to 85 that that gentleman was apparently, according to his own version of the -- had killed 70 people in about a five hour span with an automatic rifle. There is an analysis subsequently that the 70 could be 10 to 100, but 70 is the Defendant's or the accused's own statement. I don't know and I didn't know the mental capacity of the gentleman, because there's a discussion in the decision about that, but to me it is difficult to compare the situations and look at the recommendation of the Prosecution, albeit considering the mitigation issue, the remorse issue and the co-operation issue. Mr. Tadic had and has and did take advantage of his right to have a trial. We know the result. Roughly one-third of the counts were accepted by the Tribunal as guilty and the others were not guilty. I think that when we consider his right to a trial and the fact that he has exercised that right, I would ask the court to temper the fact that he has exercised that right and not punish him for doing that fact by itself. Certainly the Chamber has a right to look at all of the other facts about Mr. Tadic, the testimony, his background, things that Mr. Vujin is going to talk about, lack of a prior criminal record, his character, his individual circumstances, but I think I'm asking the court not to punish him for that one particular factor. Of course, we don't have a mitigation situation here, because there was a trial and there was a finding of guilty to some of the counts. The Defence of the accused during the trial is well-known to you. I can't comment upon that. The co-operation with the Tribunal, which I think really may have, although again I may not be 100 per cent correct -- but it seems to have played a large part in what the recommendation was by the Prosecution in that sentencing and the way that it was presented to you yesterday. I think that ties into another part of what I talked about before the break, but didn't really elaborate. I mentioned, and these are my words, your Honours, I mentioned sort of the mission of the Tribunal, which included the return of the rule of law in Bosnia, the restoration of true peace and reconciliation, and I think they talk about a collective reconciliation in another part of it. So I think the message that Mr. Niemann would like to send out is that if you co-operate, you are going to be rewarded. Whether that goes along with the mission of the Tribunal is, of course, for you to determine. However, how does Mr. Tadic fit into this bigger concept? In other words, Mr. Tadic, who is going to be sentenced here, and there will be, of course, a message that will come out of that sentence. This case again has a very high profile, whether it is in Europe -- it also has a high profile in America and other parts of the world. The message has been so far such that actually Mr. Tadic, and his case is well-known everywhere. It goes hand in hand with my colleague's comments that Mr. Tadic will never be able to sink into oblivion or disappear no matter what you do in a week or so in regard to a sentence. He will have to live with that. I submit to you that you may sentence him to a natural jail cell some place in the world, but with that notoriety he has a sort of a portable jail cell of his own that he is going to be taking with him wherever he goes because of the profile of this case. The fact that he is the first one and the fact that he was the one that got the ball rolling -- it sounds like a very trite term, but he was the one who was involved in being prosecuted by the Tribunal and whatever the message is. Now the mission of the Tribunal, and this goes again, and I am not sure if I will be able to answer this question. Judge McDonald you had -- it is only maybe my perception that you had some thoughts, and perhaps there was some -- I won't call it a struggle but an intellectual concern of whether sentencing Tadic and Tadic only means only something to Tadic and for Tadic. What about the other individuals? What about the leaders who were there in Bosnia in the small area, in the Opstina, in Banja Luka and then upward from that, and I am appreciating the struggle as I am perceiving you having -- maybe you don't, but that's what I am perceiving. What then is the message? If Tadic gets X years, does that mean that all of these folks who were there who have either sealed or unsealed indictments filed, who have been wanted, and thousands of others, how are they going to take that? Will that lead to reconciliation? Will some part of that society be happy -- that's maybe a bad word -- satisfied if there's going to be -- there's a word, you know that we use in America too much I think, and that's whether there's going to be a closure for some of the people who were involved in these awful things. I'm not here, by the way, to in any way give you information or ideas about what I think about the conflict in Bosnia or give you any specific hard information. My gosh! You have sat here and listened to the evidence. You read. You know what goes on. I guess the question is going to be: what will the message be? It's my feeling that on the basis of what this particular Chamber has made in terms of finding of guilt that Mr. Tadic deserves some sentence. Mr. Niemann said this is not the most serious. Mr. Livingston has a certain idea. I have listened to what the Yugoslav law was. We all have some ideas that in some of the countries where he could end up there are programmes, processes of parole, of remission, of pardon, of whatever other thing that possibly he can take advantage of. However, as I have looked at what he has been found guilty of and what he has spent in custody at this point, which is four and a half -- three and a half years, 41 plus months, we have to take a look at that. We also have to realise, I think, that the time in custody has been a time where he was awaiting trial. If there is any rehabilitative aspect to anything that is in the sentencing structure or scheme here, that certainly has not happened. From my vantage point he is a relatively young man. I don't know whether rehabilitation should be just thrown out the window and not considered in this case. He has done what we again in the United States call "hard time" at this point. He has been really warehoused here awaiting trial. If you look at some of the parole schemes, remissions, pardons in some of the other countries, his three and a half years spent in custody here may amount to five, six, seven or as much as ten years in some of the systems. It depends whether it is the British system, the Dutch system, the American system. So that's the equivalent that he has already spent. I am impressed with his background and the way he has handled himself. I am concerned, as Mr. Livingston is, that he has nowhere to go. I am quite concerned also that there is an additional punishment that I think may not have been mentioned, the fact that he was taken away from his family, from his daughter. I am not going to recount the testimony of his daughter. I think it was rather touching and you watched it. I think that's another type of punishment. I would ask the court to consider as punishment the time that Mr. Tadic has served so far here in Holland, and send him home wherever he can find a home, at least back to his family on July 14th. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kostic. Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, honourable Judges, honourable counsel, when the Defence begins the third part of its statement within the unified defence of our client, we wish to stress that it's very difficult for us at this point in time to discuss the circumstances, because the Defence has already given notice on its appeal on judgement and guilt. However, fully respecting the rules of this Tribunal we have to present our views on all the circumstances which are relevant for the penalty. Mr. Niemann, as the Prosecutor, the chief Prosecutor in this case, yesterday in addition to his written submission earlier on, which contains certain views, elaborated on that submission orally, adding a few more points, and if I understood him well, the position of the Prosecutor is that Mr. Tadic is not a small fish, to use their term; that he had an important part on the attack on Kozarac; that he played an active part in the expulsion of Muslims and Croats in Prijedor municipality, that after the completion of ethnic cleansing he became a political leader in Kozarac; that he was President of the Kozarac SDS; that he participated after taking part in the conflict in Kozarac; that his position became higher; that he did all this out of greed, hatred; that he was two-faced; that he was motivated by the idea of a Greater Serbia; that he was independent directly responsible for the destruction of people in Prijedor; that Mr. Tadic was not under any kind of threat so as to be forced to do all of this; and that he did all this, although he was an adult, 36, over 36 at the time; that he had a privileged status; that he was prompted by greed for violence and power; that the aim was the more there would be for the Serbs, the more there would be for Tadic; and that there is not a single mitigating circumstance, because he did not co-operate with the court; that he had a privileged and safe position in the traffic police and later in the local community; that he enjoyed certain rights with respect to the distribution of property; and that he had access to humanitarian aid. All these points are mentioned by Mr. Niemann in order to show to what extent our client was in a position to do precisely what you found him guilty of under Count 1. I must put the following question: on the basis of which evidence presented to this court does Mr. Niemann claim that our client was greedy, that he was motivated by hatred, that he was two-faced, that he was inspired by the idea of a Greater Serbia, and that he was indirectly responsible for the destruction of all people in Prijedor? I have carefully read the transcript from the hearings and I never came across a single piece of evidence in support of such points and allegations. I don't know what Mr. Niemann had in mind when he speaks of greed, because he adds the craving for power. Mr. Tadic never in his life represented power. Mr. Tadic never in his life was greedy for property. These are two kinds of greed that I must say our position about this. Mr. Tadic was never inspired by the idea of a Greater Serbia, because the idea of a Greater Serbia is used in this trial, too, and I think that that is the business of another branch of science rather than this Tribunal to deal with. However, in order to discuss this idea and see whether Tadic was inspired by this idea, we must go back to the Declaration on the Proclamation of the Republic of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina, dated 27th January 1992, which was issued after the referendum organised on 9th and 10th November 1991. Let us begin with the referendum and the role of Mr. Dusko Tadic in organising that referendum, as reference is being made to this in this Trial Chamber repeatedly. The referendum was prepared and organised not for the Serbian people, not exclusively for the Serbs to express their view. It was organised for the people who vote in the referendum to declare whether they wished to remain within a unified Bosnia-Herzegovina, within a unified Yugoslavia, which at that time was already being undermined. That is why there were two ballots, because the point of departure was the right to self-determination, and if the position of a part of the Serbs were not accepted, that is that they should remain within a unified Bosnia-Herzegovina as a federal unit of Yugoslavia, then other decisions would follow, and the results of that referendum led to the declaration which in its substantive articles contains the following: "The Republic of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina is proclaimed. The Republic is a component part of The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as a Federal Unit". There is no Serbia; there is mention of Yugoslavia only: "That the territorial delineation with the political communities of other peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well as the settlement of other rights and obligations will be done by peaceful means and by agreement, fully respecting the ethnic, historical, legal, cultural, economic, geographic, communication and other important criteria, and fully observing the principles and rules of international law. The constitution of the Republic will guarantee full equality of peoples and citizens before the law and against all forms of discrimination. The seat of the republic will be in Sarajevo". Those are some of the most important Articles of that declaration on the basis of which this Republic was proclaimed, and on the basis of which a constitution was passed in March of the same year, which reflected and mirrored this: equality of citizens and prohibition of any kind of discrimination. This position of the Serbian people, which was proclaimed and published in the Official Gazette, one cannot find anywhere the idea of a Greater Serbia, the idea on separation along ethnic lines. Nowhere can we find evidence of any kind of discrimination. Therefore, Dusko Tadic himself agreeing to participate in this kind of statement of views, working at the referendum as a member of a committee, that is the lowest level body which participated in the organisation of the referendum, because there is a main commission, then a regional commission, and then there is the voting commission. At that referendum, which was carried out under the instructions of the main commission, the election committee's task was merely to conduct the voting at the polling station and to ensure the correctness of the polling procedure. If in Kozarac and for that part of Kozarac was this polling station organised, that is the old part of the city, which was covered by the voting commission of which Mr. Tadic was the President, Mr. Tadic's role was no other than to technically implement something that was permitted at the time by the constitution. May I remind you at the time the constitution of the previous Bosnia-Herzegovina was still in force, which guaranteed the right to vote and to be elected to everyone. Therefore this was a simple matter of technical organisation and implementation of the decision of superiors. Mr. Tadic was the lowest level in this hierarchy. So to speak of his active role in organising the referendum is absolutely out of the question. So much about the referendum itself, the idea that existed and which, as we have tried to show, has nothing in common with the alleged inspiration, by the idea of Greater Serbia attributed to Dusko Tadic.
