All the witnesses that we have presented, as well as others, especially witnesses with whom Mr. Tadic had good relations, and they were of Muslim ethnicity or nationality -- let me use that term, although that is not, of course, a nationality; it is a religious affiliation, but let us avoid discussions of that kind -- such as Kemal Susic, Kahrimanovic and others, show that Mr. Tadic was never before, before all these conflicts involved in politics. Borka Rakic speaks of this on page 4453 of the transcript. She says she never discussed politics with him. Smoljic also speaks of this, who as a refugee went there and said Tadic never spoke of politics with him. Then there is the testimony of Mira Tadic, Ljubomir Tadic, the wife and brother of the accused, who know him well, who are very familiar with his activities. Therefore, up to the point in time when, because of some reason which I believe we cannot go into now at this stage, tension occurred between the members of the various ethnic groups, and when conflict appeared to be in the offing between national groups, but Muslims had already started to arm themselves, the citizens' forum was organised that many witnesses referred to, and I think that there's no doubt that Dusko Tadic participated in that forum as a Serb, as one of the few people in that delegation, one of the few Serbs, who went to Prijedor to seek to resolve the tension by peaceful means. Is the Prosecutor correct when he says that Mr. Tadic was two-faced? I think he is not, this evidence points to the opposite. Mr. Tadic had correct and good relations with Muslims, with his neighbours. He taught their children karate. His bar was visited by Muslims as by members of all other ethnic groups, and as you heard from the testimony these past few days from all the witnesses who spoke before you, he was not brought up in a nationalist spirit. His beard which he wore occasionally, as Kemal Susic says on page 2177 of the transcript, was customary at the time, and it was not an expression of any kind of nationalism or any other racial aspects of nationalism. Ms. Mira Tadic confirmed the point that after the conflict in Prijedor quite a number of Muslims stayed on in Prijedor. That assertion was confirmed by the testimony of Nashia Jakupovic on page 3157 of the transcript, who confirmed what Mira Tadic was saying, that Dusko Tadic assisted the Jakupovic family to obtain documents, as he had helped members of our families after the conflict to obtain documents, to get medicines, and he even saw some off to the station. All this was happening after the conflict in Kozarac, and I think the Prosecutor is not correct when he says that he was two-faced, that he pretended to have good relations, but basically he was full of hatred, because if that was so he would not have helped other people. Finally, there is the decision of the crisis staff, which says that the crisis staff decided to oppose all attempts of forcible, of displacement of the population under any kind of pressure and that it would prevent any such possible attempts by all legal means. Therefore, there was no idea to displace anyone by force: you cannot observe the events in Prijedor in isolation when examining in whole issue. You will have to link this to what was happening in Jajca, for instance, in Zenica, what was happening in Tuzla. There you had an identical situation in the opposite sense. Columns of Serbs were moving out of those towns, leaving all their property behind, not because they were expelled, but because the balance of forces was such that they had to move out so that during the conflict grave consequences would not be suffered by them and members of their families. It is in this light that we have to observe the events in the surroundings of Prijedor, and then it is quite easy to establish what Tadic's role was in all this. I submit that Tadic had no role in this that could be interpreted as him having organised deportations and the displacement of Muslims by force. What did Tadic gain during the war for one to be able to say that he was greedy? He didn't get anything. His family was left without a breadwinner. His family was a refugee family. They had the status of refugees in Banja Luka. To this day they are living in a rented apartment. They have no apartment of their own, because they were evicted from their apartment. What is it, what evidence do we have to justify such an allegation of the Prosecution? My submission is that there is not a single piece of evidence to corroborate this. What I was saying a moment ago regarding the relations between Mr. Tadic and the Muslims after the conflict, when he helped them and gave them medicine and helped them to obtain documents, this gives me the right to claim that on the basis of what we have said from the testimony on the relationships he had with his Muslim neighbours, on his upbringing, that there wasn't the slightest trace of hatred for anyone because he may be a Croat or a Muslim. Anyway, you have been able to hear the testimony of a witness who described what their friendship was like, though she was a Croat. A great deal has been said about Mr. Tadic as a man, a good man and a good neighbour, and especially I wish to underline once again the statement of Kemal Susic, his teacher from his fifth year of elementary school, according to his testimony, who followed his growing up and who said that throughout he was a good person. Therefore, against this backdrop and this kind of family circumstances no hatred could have been born in Mr. Tadic, and further on no justification to allege that he was two-faced, because I go back to what I have said, that his friendly feelings, his good relations with the Muslims, were evidenced by his behaviour after the conflict. Then there is the question of indirect responsibility for destruction of people and for persecution under Count 1. I think there is a great danger lurking here. The danger that we might develop a concept that is not in accordance with the rules of this Tribunal. I think that we must establish individual responsibility with the utmost care, as was done for all the other counts of the indictment. In this way we have put in one count something for which we do not have evidence. You have found evidence. We must accept your decision and your determination, of course. I'm talking now about the degree of criminal responsibility specifically in relation to Dusko Tadic's role in the broader picture. I have been speaking about his political activity so far, saying that it was reduced to a minimum, to a technical role of implementing something that others had decided. This is evidenced through his activities in the Red Cross and his activities in the local commune. It should be noted, and I think that you realise this, after Professor Aleksic's testimony, that the local commune, which is at this point not even a constitutional category, is simply a small part of a municipality which has the right to self-organise itself. The citizens get together and say: "We need a department store or a supermarket because the other one we have is too far, 4 kms away". So they get together and decide that at an assembly meeting. All they can do is submit a request to the municipality and then it is up to the municipality to decide whether it has the funds, whether it will be done, whether this fits into the town plan and many other things like that. Therefore, the local commune has no right of decision-making, and will be the secretary of that local commune, who is not even an official organ, has absolutely no rights. He is simply a person who is employed on the basis of a competition just like any other staff member in a bank. Therefore, his role as secretary of the local commune, which according to the position of the Prosecution gave him some kind of a privileged position is unfounded. There is no authority that he acquired. There is nothing. The work of Mr. Tadic as a reserve policeman in the traffic police is not evidence of any privileged position, because you had hundreds of other traffic policemen at the same time, who certainly did not have any privileged position. Simply there was the need to organise this service, to check the traffic in an abnormal situation that the country was in at the time. Therefore, there is no privileged position of Tadic. Would anyone who was privileged by the authorities be evicted from his apartment together with his family? If Tadic had been a person of importance, he would have been given a house of his own or an apartment in the best possible place rather than being evicted and his apartment being given to somebody else, according to some kind of rules. The Prosecutor says that there are no mitigating circumstances, because he did not co-operate with the court, and he had access to humanitarian aid and control over the distribution of property. I must tell you that Mr. Dusko Tadic, as the secretary of the local commune, as a Red Cross activist, did not play any role in deciding about who would settle in Kozarac. He was the person who for the people who had come back or who were refugees from other areas and came to settle there, he just distributed the relief that he received from the Red Cross. We have tendered as evidence a document about this, which we didn't manage to translate in full, but I hope it is quite clear from that document that it's a list on the basis of which humanitarian relief was distributed, goods, food, detergents and other products, and which was delivered on the basis of an invoice that has been submitted. When the truck arrives, then Tadic had the role to distribute it, together with the other members of the commission, not alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I wonder if I can ask you a question on that? To the limited extent to which I was able, I looked at the first names of the people to whom food was distributed. Would I be right in thinking that none of them were Muslim names?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: I think that that is true, your Honour, but there are Croat names. There are Croat names. That is one of the lists. Unfortunately the lists no longer exist. We managed to find this particular list. You saw the testimony that we gave you in written form by Mr. Cavic, who said that precisely because of this distribution of humanitarian aid and food that people objected, because Tadic had given aid to Muslims, too, then the people had complained why he hadn't been taken to the front. Have a look at that statement. That's what it says. So a witness spoke of this, too, that there was an elderly woman and a few younger people, Muslims, a few younger men who received assistance, aid like all others. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, in that part also he did not play a role which was over-important. These are circumstances which will assist you, in my deep conviction, to put Dusko Tadic within a realistic framework of his obligations and his rights which he practically didn't have, except for the right to carry out his duties in line with the statute of the municipality, the statute of the local community, etc. So his work was found by the regulations and decisions of other organs. This is very important, in my opinion, because the Prosecutor keeps insisting on big fish, small fish, the level of criminal liability, etc. I shall also recall the dates when the decisions were passed to restart the local community, when he was appointed secretary. This was August 1992 and it was constituted on 15th August, and the secretary was appointed on 9th November. November 1992, so when the fighting broke out, when we are talking about May and April and the preceding months, when the situation was becoming complicated, Dusko Tadic was not even that. He wasn't the secretary of the local commune. He wasn't an activist, etc. May I also recall that before the conflict broke out, Dusko Tadic was not the President of the SDS for Kozarac. At that time when these events were taking place Kozarac didn't even have an SDS organisation. According to the statute of the SDS, 150 members were needed in order to establish an organisation. At that time in Kozarac there weren't 150 members, so an organisation could not be established, a local organisation within the local community. Dusko Tadic at that point in time, because he was outside the organisation, and he only had a member card of the SDS, did not take part in the work of any organisation of the SDS, nor could he present certain views, positions, ideas or accept them. This happened only later, when he was indeed appointed secretary, but you will note in the evidence you have in this respect that there is one person who is missing for this committee, because they were supposed to elect 15 members and they only had 14, but the activity of the SDS and the activities of the local community, according to all the evidence tendered, the testimonies of the witnesses and the written testimonies, boils down to bringing life back to Kozarac. The health centre was rebuilt and you managed to see that it started functioning again through the great efforts of Mr. Tadic, and a doctor came back there to work for a month or two or three under very difficult conditions, because all the medical equipment was taken back to the Opstina, and Ms. Tadic also testified that, because she is employed by the health centre, and she knew what happened to this equipment. Houses were repaired. Life was brought back to the village. That is where this active role is. Even now, when you walk through that area, everybody will tell you that Dusko Tadic played a major role in this respect, and everybody is surprised at what has happened to him. These are some of the reasons that are presented by the Defence in response to the allegations made by the Prosecutor in this connection. I am sorry. I will take a bit longer than our usual time, and you said that that would be all right, but it won't be very long. Finally, I wish to speak about what has been part -- is there any problem?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We may or may not. Let us see how much longer you have. We may adjourn at 5.30. You may proceed, Mr. Vujin.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that I will be completed after 20 minutes at a maximum, because I'm talking about my last point now, the application of law. I wish to draw your attention to what we tried to clarify yesterday with the Professor, too, which is relevant to the rules and procedure of this court, namely Rule 24 and Rule 101. Both rules say that sentence will be imposed in view of the gravity of the offence and also in view of the court practice of the former Yugoslavia. I'm afraid that the rules concerned are quite incomplete, and there will be quite a few problems involved, because there are going to be different interpretations. Rule C under Rule 101 speaks of whether multiple sentences shall be served consecutively or concurrently. So since my colleagues spoke of this, I shall make no further reference to it, but if we take into account customary practice of Yugoslav courts, then the provisions of paragraph C would not be applicable, although in certain cases this may serve to the benefit of the convicted person. What am I trying to say? I'm trying to say that according to our law, Yugoslav law, and that is how I interpret this provision, you are not bound by Yugoslav law, but you are bound by the practice of Yugoslav courts, and the practice of Yugoslav courts is derived from Yugoslav laws, and practice cannot be different from what the law says in terms of the practical implementation of the laws. Why am I saying this? Because you have found Mr. Dusko Tadic guilty on certain counts, having concluded that he committed crimes against humanity and violation of laws and customs of war. These are two incriminations which were committed on certain counts through the same actions. According to our legislation this is impossible, because the graver offence subsumes the lesser offence. It is possible for offences to be committed by one single action and to have two different qualifications very, very rarely in terms of a very, very specifically denominated way in which a crime was committed. When speaking of crimes against humanity, the list according to the statute of this Tribunal, murder, rape, depredation, etc., you have contained in point one of your verdict all of this, and in addition to that, that on which you found Dusko Tadic guilty according to the other counts. So according to our criminal law it would be impossible for Dusko Tadic to be found guilty for crimes against humanity and the laws and customs of war. Another thing I wish to draw your attention to is the fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you a moment? It is very important as you speak of the law in your country you tell us what country you are talking about. If you are talking about Federal law, tell us what time. Also you must refer us to a particular Article of the Code. Then when you speak of practice, if you have evidence of the practice, that must be provided, because it's very difficult for the Judges to accept just assertions of counsel unless you direct us to something that we can put our hands on, so to speak. Now, are you saying, though, that for example, in counts 5 through 11 if Mr. Tadic were found guilty for committing those acts and the Trial Chamber found that they constitute crimes against humanity, and found that they also constitute a violation of the laws or customs of war, are you saying that that finding is contrary to Yugoslav law, and, if so, you need to refer me to a particular article or section of the Yugoslav criminal code. That's one scenario. I may misunderstand you, though, because you may be saying that Count 1 only charges crimes against humanity, and Mr. Livingston said that if you look at it, temporarily at least it covers a period through May to December and all of the acts charged in the other counts for which the Trial Chamber found Mr. Tadic guilty occurred during that period and then that subsumes the other counts, but he was talking about factually. Then you speak of it legally, but more in terms of sentencing, so that you sentence for the gravest offence and you would sentence for no more; if you are going to sentence concurrently, then the sentence imposed for the greatest, which presumably would be Count 1. Those are three different scenarios. I am mostly concerned with findings of guilt for findings against humanity, for laws and customs of war for the same crimes. May we sentence X number of years for humanity and X number of years for laws and customs of war in accordance with the Yugoslav code in operation at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: That is part of the problem. I said that misunderstandings were involved in terms of the systems involved. In Article 24 of the statute and Rule 101 it doesn't say at all that you will take into account the rules -- rather the practice of courts of other countries, but precisely the court practice of the former Yugoslavia. To clarify a certain situation related to your question, first of all I am speaking about the application of the Yugoslav criminal law, the general section which was applicable when the events concerned were taking place. So that could be a starting point for you as a court to accept these provisions. I draw your attention once again to something I said, which was accepted by Mr. Keegan, that Bosnia-Herzegovina took over the provisions of the previous criminal law of Yugoslavia as their provisions. I also have to draw your attention to the fact that in the former Yugoslavia at that time there was Federal legislation, the Federal criminal law, which gave the basic provisions what a crime was, what self-defence was, etc., etc., and a special part which contained certain criminal offences and Chapter 16 deals with those offences that were included in Yugoslav law on the basis of certain international conventions and that also applied to the acts that we are discussing here today. In addition to the Federal Law, which was applied throughout the territory of the former Yugoslavia, we also had the criminal laws, codes, the republics, Montenegro, Serbia, Montenegro. Special criminal offences were stipulated there in respect to certain crimes. Murder, fights, etc. Why am I saying all of this? Because the Federal Law applied to throughout Yugoslavia and all the new states took over that lot even after secession, Slovenia, Croatia and that also happened in the case of Bosnia-Herzegovina, too. They took over this general law as their own and also their own specific law from before as their current law, too. I also wish to draw your attention to Article 4 of that law, too, that the law applied is always the softer law. So until the trial, if the law is changed by the time the trial is held, and if a milder sentence is envisaged by the new law, the new law will always be applied, not the law that was applied the time the act was committed. This is a general provision which is included in the criminal code which was taken over by Bosnia-Herzegovina and that is why I draw your attention to that again, because, as we said in connection with the death penalty, too -- let us not discuss the death penalty at length. I believe it does not exist, because we received papers, documents from Bosnia-Herzegovina. It does not exist there, so the maximum sentence is 15 years, so we take as a point of departure 15 years. I have to draw your attention to another legal institute which was not regulated by law but has been confirmed and accepted in practice. That is the so-called construction of extended criminal act. Some acts, like those from this chapter and the statute from the Tribunal by their very nature and by our criminal theory, are extended crimes. What does that mean? As you have said in Count 1, Dusko Tadic is responsible for rape, etc., etc., and you did not find him personally responsible for a certain rape, etc., etc. So you took all of that and put it into Count 1, but if you put all of that into Count 1, then all the rest, people were taken out of a column, beaten up, etc., according to our legislation would fall under this one count, because a crime against humanity can only be carried out through the commission of one act, regardless of whether you said now, as you established in Count 1, for example, for what he was responsible for May to July and then an interruption, and then from October to December. There cannot be two acts. All of it is one act. To make it clearer through an example which will familiarise you with this institute, for example, if a thief committed five thefts in a certain neighbourhood during one night or five nights and he robbed one house or five houses, these are not going to be five thefts according to our law but only one theft. Perhaps the very number concerned could only influence the sentencing, but I underline that this is practice which is applied not only in our case but also in Bosnia and Croatia and everywhere. There are many such court decisions. The Defence thought that you might have been familiar with this. I don't have this available at this point in time, not right now, but perhaps I can find these decisions for you and have them provided to you tomorrow, but that is important, that all these acts that are committed in one period of time can only be considered to be one act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I think that question has been answered or perhaps I do not understand the answer. Let me just say this. You have offered an expert witness, the Professor. He has testified about the practices. The Prosecution has offered written documents, which the Professor indicated, your witness, were dated, because they ceased as of 1988, as I recall. That is the type of evidence that we need. The representations of counsel are -- we accept them as representations of counsel, and that's why we have invited the parties to submit information regarding the sentencing practices in the former Yugoslavia. I don't know that my question is answered yet. I asked the Professor, though, yesterday, and I thought that his answer was that well, he couldn't really think of a crime like that in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia where there were different elements for two different crimes, and both crimes were charged as a result of one set of facts. He couldn't think of that, but I thought he was saying to me that if those were different elements, then that would be acceptable, but maybe I misunderstood him. Maybe it wasn't that clear. That is a problem that we have. It's now 5.30, I think we will have to adjourn. I do want, though, my question answered regarding nullem crimen ... lege, and I guess you will. That is what is the effect of what appears to be the authority under the rules to sentence for a life term, yet there not being a life term available in any of the States of the former Yugoslavia at the time of the occurrence of the acts. Now you have just, though, referred to a principle of the law changes --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Life imprisonment does not exist now either. Milder law is applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The Professor yesterday said the new law will probably call for life imprisonment in light of the abolishment of the death penalty and now that the death penalty is abolished by the constitution, you cannot use the 20 years maximum, but he spoke of differences between Serbia and Montenegro, as I recall. If you can, tomorrow please provide your opinion at least as to the nullem crimen problem, as I see it, and the other question in terms of sentencing for two crimes that have different elements, but both of them are based on the same offence, and what would be the practice in the former Yugoslavia. If it is specifically provided in the Code, the Federal Code or any of the Republics' Code, we would need a citation to that. If the answer is supported by practice, then we would need some support for that in the form of court decisions or something other than the representations of counsel. I think that would help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: That is indeed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Vujin, when you are provided with the transcript, if you will review the questions that I have asked five minutes ago and tomorrow if you could provide an answer, I will appreciate it, and also input from the Prosecution as well. You will have an opportunity to respond, because it's very important. As I indicated, Mr. Tadic, if he wishes, will have an opportunity to speak on his behalf, if he wishes, and that would be tomorrow either before or after Dr Nedopil completes his offering. You will complete your submissions but we do need some input with respect to these questions, and we will hear from the Prosecution as well as to these questions. We will then hear from Dr Nedopil or perhaps Mr. Tadic, however you wish to handle it, and that will then complete our pre-sentencing hearing tomorrow. We will not be able to begin, though, until 11.30, because there is be an initial appearance. So we will adjourn until tomorrow at 11.30. (5.35 pm)
